sub: A story about a great flood, a boat filled with animals, and a promise written in the sky. Read the clues, trace what happened in order, and prove your thinking from the text.

brief.label: Your mission
brief.h: Follow the story — then prove its theme
brief.p: You are studying this as a story, just like you would study any tale about someone given a big task. Notice how the events are ordered and what the story teaches. Back up every answer with evidence from the clues — not what you already know.

win.p: You traced the events in order, named the theme, and used real clues to back up your thinking. That is how good readers analyze a story.

clues.title: Noah gets instructions
clues.body: In the story from Genesis, God sees that people are behaving badly and decides to send a great flood. God tells Noah — described as a good man — to build a large boat called an ark and to bring his family and two of every kind of animal on board.

clues.title: Noah builds and loads
clues.body: The story says Noah does exactly what he is told. He builds the ark to the measurements given, gathers the animals, and loads his family. Noah follows every instruction without arguing.

clues.title: The waters rise
clues.body: Rain falls for forty days and forty nights. The flood covers the land. Noah, his family, and the animals stay safe inside the ark while the waters rise.

clues.title: Testing the waters
clues.body: After the rain stops, Noah sends out a dove to look for dry land. At first the dove comes back — there is nowhere to land. The second time, the dove returns with an olive branch, a sign that land is appearing.

clues.title: A rainbow and a deal
clues.body: When the flood is over, Noah and his family leave the ark. The story says God makes a covenant — a solemn promise — never to flood the whole earth again. A rainbow appears as the sign of that promise.

clues.title: True, but off-topic
clues.body: The wettest place on Earth gets about 467 inches of rain every year. That is a true weather fact — but it has nothing to do with what the Noah story is teaching about promises and fresh starts.

locks.title: Put the story in order
locks.q: Tap the three key events from the Noah story in the ORDER the text tells them.
locks.reason: The story moves in this order: Noah builds and loads the ark, then the flood rises, then the rainbow appears as a promise. Sequence helps readers see how a narrative is structured.

locks.title: Name the theme
locks.q: What idea does the Noah story MOST clearly teach?
options: Doing what you are asked leads to a fresh start and a new promise
Rain is dangerous and people should always carry umbrellas
Boats must be built to exact measurements
locks.reason: Clues 1, 2, and 5 all show Noah obeying, surviving, and receiving a promise — the story's theme is about faithfulness leading to a new beginning. The other options are either off-topic or too small.

locks.title: Gather strong evidence
locks.q: Check every clue that is STRONG evidence for the theme 'doing what you are asked leads to a fresh start.' Leave out the true-but-off-topic fact.

items.t: Noah follows every instruction and builds the ark
The flood clears the land and Noah's family survives safely
The wettest place on Earth gets 467 inches of rain a year
God makes a rainbow promise that the earth will get a fresh start

locks.reason: The rain-record fact is true but completely off-topic. Strong evidence must actually connect to what the story is teaching — obedience, survival, and a new promise.

locks.title: Name the source book
locks.q: The Noah story comes from the first book of the Hebrew Bible. Clue 1 names it. Type that book's name.
locks.reason: Clue 1 tells us the story comes from Genesis, the first book of the Hebrew Bible. Knowing the source book is part of reading any text in context.

sub: A story about running away from a job, a giant fish, and getting to try again. Read the clues, find the cause and effect, and prove the theme with evidence.

brief.label: Your mission
brief.h: Trace cause-and-effect — then name the theme
brief.p: You are reading the story of Jonah as literature — a tale about what happens when someone runs from a responsibility and then gets a second chance. Look for what causes what, and use only the clues to back up your answers.

win.p: You found the cause-and-effect chain and named the theme. Noticing how events connect is a key skill for reading any story.

clues.title: Jonah gets a job
clues.body: In the story from the Book of Jonah, God tells Jonah to go to the city of Nineveh and warn the people there. Jonah does not want to go. Instead of heading to Nineveh, he boards a ship going in the opposite direction.

clues.title: A storm at sea
clues.body: A violent storm hits the ship. The sailors are terrified. Jonah tells them that the storm is happening because of him — he is running away from his task. The sailors throw Jonah into the sea, and the storm stops.

clues.title: Swallowed whole
clues.body: The story says a great fish swallows Jonah. He is inside the fish for three days and three nights. There, Jonah prays and decides to go back and do what he was asked.

clues.title: The second chance
clues.body: The fish spits Jonah onto dry land. God tells Jonah a second time to go to Nineveh. This time Jonah goes. He delivers the message, and the people of Nineveh change their ways.

clues.title: Where this story lives
clues.body: The Book of Jonah is a short book in the Hebrew Bible, studied here as a piece of literature. Scholars note that it focuses on themes of mercy and second chances — ideas that appear across many world stories.

clues.title: True, but off-topic
clues.body: The Pacific Ocean is so wide that it covers about one-third of the entire surface of the Earth. That is a true geography fact — but it has nothing to do with what the Jonah story is teaching about mercy and second chances.

locks.title: Name the theme
locks.q: What theme does the Jonah story MOST clearly teach?
options: Running from a responsibility leads to trouble, but a second chance is possible
Oceans are too dangerous for anyone to sail
Fish are the most important animals in the sea
locks.reason: Clues 1 through 4 trace Jonah running away, facing consequences, and then being given another chance — the classic second-chance theme. The ocean and fish options pull from details, not the story's teaching.

locks.title: Trace the cause and effect
locks.q: Tap the three events in the ORDER they happen in the story.
locks.reason: The story's order is: Jonah runs away, then is swallowed by the fish, then finally goes to Nineveh. This cause-and-effect chain shows how the story builds its theme.

locks.title: Gather the evidence
locks.q: Check every clue that is STRONG evidence for the theme 'running away leads to trouble, but a second chance is possible.' Leave out the true-but-off-topic fact.

items.t: Jonah boards a ship going the wrong direction and a storm hits
Jonah spends three days in the fish and decides to obey
The Pacific Ocean covers one-third of Earth's surface
God gives Jonah a second chance and he succeeds in Nineveh

locks.reason: The Pacific Ocean fact is true but has nothing to do with the story's theme. Good readers pick only the clues that directly connect to what the text is teaching.

locks.title: Name the collection
locks.q: Clue 5 names the larger collection the Book of Jonah belongs to. Type two words for it.
locks.reason: Clue 5 says the Book of Jonah is in the Hebrew Bible. Knowing where a text comes from — its source — helps us read it fairly as literature.

sub: A short story Jesus tells in the Gospel of Luke. Who really counts as a neighbor? Read the clues, find the evidence, and prove your answer from the text.

brief.label: Your mission
brief.h: Find who helps — and what that teaches
brief.p: You are studying this as a literary parable — a short story with a big idea inside it. Your job is to notice who acts, who doesn't, and what the story teaches about neighbors. Use only the clues to back up your answers.

win.p: You found the theme, gathered real evidence, and named the source. That is exactly how readers analyze a short story with a lesson inside it.

clues.title: A man is hurt
clues.body: In the parable told by Jesus in the Gospel of Luke, a man is traveling on the road from Jerusalem to Jericho when robbers attack him, beat him, and leave him badly hurt on the side of the road.

clues.title: The first passerby
clues.body: A priest — a religious leader — comes down the road and sees the hurt man. The story says the priest crosses to the other side and keeps walking. He does not stop to help.

clues.title: The second passerby
clues.body: Next, a Levite — another religious figure — comes by. He also sees the hurt man, crosses to the other side, and walks on without helping.

clues.title: The unexpected helper
clues.body: A Samaritan — someone from a group that many people of that time did not get along with — comes by next. He sees the hurt man, stops, bandages his wounds, puts him on his own animal, brings him to an inn, and pays for his care. The story makes the outsider the hero.

clues.title: Where this story lives
clues.body: This parable appears in the Gospel of Luke, one of the four Gospels in the New Testament of the Christian Bible. It is told as a story Jesus uses to answer a question: 'Who is my neighbor?'

clues.title: True, but off-topic
clues.body: The ancient road from Jerusalem to Jericho dropped about 3,300 feet in elevation over roughly 17 miles. That is a true fact about geography — but it is not what the parable is teaching about neighbors and helping.

locks.title: Name the theme
locks.q: What does the Good Samaritan parable MOST clearly teach?
options: A true neighbor is the person who actually stops and helps — even an outsider
Long roads are always dangerous and people should not travel alone
Religious leaders are always the best people to call for help
locks.reason: Clues 2, 3, and 4 show that the religious leaders pass by while the Samaritan — an outsider — is the one who helps. The story answers 'who is a neighbor?' by showing action, not group membership.

locks.title: Gather the evidence
locks.q: Check every clue that is STRONG evidence for the theme 'a true neighbor is anyone who stops to help.' Leave out the true-but-off-topic fact.

items.t: The priest sees the hurt man but crosses to the other side
The Samaritan stops, bandages, and pays for the hurt man's care
The road from Jerusalem to Jericho drops 3,300 feet in elevation
The Levite also passes by without helping

locks.reason: The elevation fact is true geography but tells us nothing about who a neighbor is. The three strong clues all show who helps and who does not — that is the evidence the story actually builds on.

locks.title: Name the source
locks.q: Clue 5 names the Gospel this parable comes from. Type that Gospel's name.
locks.reason: Clue 5 says the parable is in the Gospel of Luke. Naming the source is part of studying any text fairly — it helps us know what kind of writing we are reading.

locks.title: Order the passersby
locks.q: Tap the three people who come down the road in the ORDER the story introduces them.
locks.reason: The story introduces them in this order: the Priest, then the Levite, then the Samaritan. The order matters — the reader expects a pattern of passing by, which makes the Samaritan's help even more striking.

sub: A famous set of rules from the Book of Exodus. What do they say, where do they come from, and what kind of text are they? Read the clues and unlock the answers.

brief.label: Your mission
brief.p: You are studying the Ten Commandments as a legal and literary text — a list of rules from an ancient story. Your job is to notice what kind of text it is, what it contains, and where it comes from. Use only the clues to back up every answer.

win.p: You identified the text type, named the source, and gathered real evidence. Readers who notice what KIND of text they are reading understand it much better.

clues.title: Moses goes up
clues.body: In the story from the Book of Exodus, Moses leads the Israelites through the desert after leaving Egypt. The story says Moses climbs Mount Sinai, where he receives a set of laws from God written on two stone tablets.

clues.title: What the list says
clues.body: The Ten Commandments are a list of rules. Some deal with how to relate to God — for example, not worshipping other gods and keeping one day a week as a rest day. Others deal with how to treat people — for example, do not steal, do not lie, and honor your parents.

clues.title: Written in stone
clues.body: The story describes the commandments as written on two stone tablets. Moses carries them down the mountain. In the story, having rules written on stone is a way of showing they are meant to last.

clues.title: A list of laws
clues.body: Unlike a parable or a poem, the Ten Commandments are a legal text — a set of rules and instructions. Many ancient cultures created written law codes. Studying this text as literature means noticing what kind of writing it is and how it is organized.

clues.title: Where this text lives
clues.body: The Ten Commandments appear in the Book of Exodus, the second book of the Hebrew Bible. The word 'exodus' means departure or going out — the book is named for the Israelites' journey out of Egypt.

clues.title: True, but off-topic
clues.body: The Sinai Peninsula, where the story is set, is a real place — a triangular piece of land between Africa and Asia. The desert there can reach temperatures above 100°F. That is a true geography fact — but it is not what the Exodus story is teaching about laws and rules.

locks.title: What kind of text is it?
locks.q: Based on the clues, what TYPE of writing are the Ten Commandments?
options: A legal text — a set of rules and instructions
A poem written in rhyming verses
A parable — a short story with a hidden lesson
locks.reason: Clue 4 directly says the Ten Commandments are a legal text — a list of rules. Clues 2 and 3 support this by describing the list's contents and its format (written on stone). Noticing text type is a key reading skill.

locks.title: Gather evidence about the text
locks.q: Check every clue that gives STRONG information about what the Ten Commandments say or where they come from. Leave out the true-but-off-topic fact.

items.t: The commandments cover both how to relate to God and how to treat other people
The rules are written on two stone tablets brought down from Mount Sinai
The Sinai desert can reach temperatures above 100°F
The text appears in the Book of Exodus, the second book of the Hebrew Bible

locks.reason: The desert temperature fact is true geography but tells us nothing about what the commandments say or where they come from. The three strong clues all come directly from what the text says and where it lives.

locks.title: Name the source book
locks.q: Clue 5 names the book where the Ten Commandments appear. Type that book's name.
locks.reason: Clue 5 tells us the Ten Commandments appear in the Book of Exodus. The clue also tells us what the word means — naming and understanding a source is part of reading any text in context.

locks.title: Order the key events
locks.q: Tap the three events from the Moses story in the ORDER the text presents them.
locks.reason: The story's order is: the Israelites journey through the desert, then Moses goes up the mountain, then he brings the tablets back down. Sequence helps readers follow how a narrative builds to its key moment.

h1: The Last Supper: Text and Painting
sub: Leonardo da Vinci painted a famous scene from a Gospel story. But what does the TEXT say — and what did the PAINTING add? Read the clues and separate art from scripture.

brief.label: Your mission
brief.h: Separate what the text says from what the painting shows
brief.p: You are doing two things at once: reading a Gospel passage as literature AND looking at a famous Renaissance painting as art history. Your job is to notice what the text actually says versus what Leonardo chose to show. Use only the clues — no outside knowledge needed.

win.p: You found what the Gospel says, what the painting adds, and where both come from. Comparing a text with a visual interpretation of it is a powerful reading and art-history skill.

clues.title: What the Gospel says
clues.body: In the Gospel of John (and also in the other three Gospels), Jesus shares a final meal with his twelve disciples. During the meal, the text says Jesus tells them that one of them will betray him. The disciples react with shock and sadness.

clues.title: Leonardo's version
clues.body: About 1,400 years after the Gospel was written, Leonardo da Vinci painted The Last Supper on a wall in Milan, Italy, around 1495–1498. The painting shows the moment just after Jesus announces the betrayal. Leonardo arranged all thirteen figures in a single row along a table, with Jesus at the center.

clues.title: Groups of three
clues.body: In Leonardo's painting, the twelve disciples are arranged in four groups of three on either side of Jesus. Their faces and hand gestures show different reactions — shock, denial, curiosity. This grouping and the varied expressions are choices Leonardo made as an artist; the Gospel text does not describe the disciples grouped this way.

clues.title: What the text adds that the painting doesn't show
clues.body: The Gospel text includes spoken words — Jesus says 'one of you will betray me.' It also includes a moment where a disciple asks who the betrayer is. These spoken words and questions are in the text, but a painting can only show one frozen moment. Leonardo chose the moment of shocked reaction.

clues.title: Where each comes from
clues.body: The story comes from the Gospels in the New Testament of the Christian Bible — especially the Gospel of John. Leonardo's painting is now in Milan, Italy, and is considered one of the most famous artworks of the Renaissance period (roughly 1300–1600 CE).

clues.title: True, but off-topic
clues.body: Leonardo painted The Last Supper using tempera and oil on a dry plaster wall — not the wet-plaster fresco method used by most Renaissance painters. This unusual technique caused the paint to start flaking within years. That is a true art-history fact about materials — but it is not what the story or the painting is teaching about the Last Supper scene.

locks.title: What does the TEXT say that the painting cannot?
locks.q: Which of these is something the GOSPEL TEXT tells us that a painting cannot show?
options: The words Jesus spoke — 'one of you will betray me'
The number of people at the table
The way Leonardo arranged the disciples in groups of three
locks.reason: Clue 4 explains this directly: the text includes spoken words and dialogue that a painting — which captures only one moment — cannot show. The other options come from the painting, not the text.

locks.title: Gather the evidence
locks.q: Check every clue that tells us something SPECIFIC about what the Gospel text says OR what Leonardo added. Leave out the true-but-off-topic paint fact.

items.t: The Gospel text says Jesus tells his disciples one of them will betray him
Leonardo arranged the disciples in four groups of three — a choice not in the text
Leonardo used tempera on dry plaster, which caused flaking within years
Leonardo painted the moment of shocked reaction after Jesus' announcement

locks.reason: The flaking-paint fact is a true art-history detail about materials — it tells us nothing about what the text says or how the painting interprets the scene. The three strong clues all connect directly to the text or the painting's artistic choices.

locks.title: Order what happens in the Gospel story
locks.q: Tap the three moments from the Gospel account in the ORDER the text tells them.

pads.e: ❓ A disciple asks who the betrayer is
🍞 Jesus shares the meal and speaks

locks.reason: The Gospel text moves in this order: Jesus speaks at the meal, the disciples react with shock, then a disciple asks who the betrayer is. Understanding the sequence helps readers see what Leonardo chose to freeze in paint.

locks.title: Name the source
locks.q: Clue 5 names the collection that includes the Gospel accounts of this meal. Type two words: the New ___.
locks.reason: Clue 5 says the Gospels are in the New Testament of the Christian Bible. Knowing the source — both for the text and for the painting — is what makes it possible to compare them fairly.
